articles.title: Brewing nor’easter to stir up days of trouble for the Outer Banks and Mid-Atlantic
articles.summary: Strong winds, pounding seas and coastal flood threats will be near-constant companions for parts of North Carolina up through the Chesapeake Bay area as a coastal storm that’s expected to linger well into next week starts to take shape this weekend.
articles.body: Strong winds, pounding seas and coastal flood threats will be near-constant companions for parts of North Carolina up through the Chesapeake Bay area this weekend as a nor’easter that’s expected to linger well into next week starts to take shape. This budding storm will not follow in the exact footsteps or reach the same strength as last month’s nor’easter. Still, it’s not going to be a pleasant few days for the areas impacted by the new storm. Here’s what to expect. Wind and rain Wind will be the most widespread and long-lasting threat. Windy conditions will start to pick up later Saturday afternoon after a potent cold front slices through the Mid-Atlantic and eastern North Carolina and brings a major cooldown and some rain. Frequent gusts of 30 to 40 mph are possible once the front moves through the Chesapeake Bay and inland eastern North Carolina. Stronger gusts up to 50 mph are possible for North Carolina’s Outer Banks. Winds will worsen once the area of low pressure that will become the coastal storm starts to develop off the North Carolina coast Sunday. Gusts up to 60 mph are possible in parts of the Outer Banks by Sunday afternoon, with gusts approaching 50 mph farther inland in the state and up into parts of coastal Virginia and Maryland. These winds could bring down trees or power lines and lead to some power outages. This increase in wind speed is due to an interaction between the developing storm and an area of high pressure in southeastern Canada. These two will squeeze the air between them, sending faster winds at the coast. The stronger the storm gets, the higher the wind speeds will climb. This budding storm isn’t expected to become super powerful, but its proximity to the coast elevates its wind threat. The nor’easter will likely be fully formed by Monday afternoon, which is also when wind speeds will start to peak for the coast and rain will start to spread over the region. Flash flooding isn’t a significant threat, but wind-driven rain will not be pleasant to be out and about in. Gusts of more than 60 mph are possible in parts of the Outer Banks with 40 to 50 mph gusts creeping toward the Interstate 95 corridor in North Carolina and southern Virginia. Farther north along the coast, gusts to 30 mph are possible in parts of coastal Delaware and New Jersey even as the storm remains near the Carolinas. Similarly strong winds are possible on Tuesday in North Carolina and the Mid-Atlantic and may ease only slightly by Wednesday. The forecast for the latter half of next week is more uncertain and will depend heavily on exactly how long the coastal storm meanders near the Carolinas. Regardless, breezy to windy conditions along the coast could continue into next weekend. Coastal flooding This is another one of the storm’s prolonged threats. At least minor coastal flooding could start as early as Sunday morning’s high tide in parts of the Outer Banks and up through the Chesapeake Bay, as strong winds shove more water ashore. Water levels will rise higher by Sunday afternoon’s high tide and some areas could experience moderate coastal flooding at that time, especially around the Virginia-North Carolina border. Further instances of moderate flooding are likely during Monday’s high tides and a similar rhythm of issues will continue through at least midweek. Some spots could see major flooding depending on exactly how close the storm hugs the coast. Hand-in-hand with coastal flood threats, rough seas and larger waves are likely to pound the coast later this weekend and well into next week. Days of this relentless wave action could worsen ongoing beach erosion, especially in parts of the Outer Banks, where homes have crumbled into the sea in recent years and roadways have washed away. Will this storm be tropical? Once the coastal storm forms off the coast of the Carolinas, it’s forecast to linger there for several days and potentially up to a week. This storm will not be a tropical system when it forms: Tropical storms are fueled by warm water, whereas this one will get its start along the same cold front that ushers in this weekend’s cooldown. However, the longer it lingers over warm water located just off the coast, a chance starts to creep in that it could become a hybrid system — fed by both the ocean heat and energy in the atmosphere. The storm is unlikely to become tropical, but it’s not impossible later next week. If it did, the impacts wouldn’t change much; the National Hurricane Center would just have to keep an eye on it.

articles.title: More NHS staff sacked over Nottingham attacks victims' records
articles.summary: Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust says a new system will be brought in to protect records.
articles.body:
Further members of staff have been sacked by an NHS trust for inappropriately accessing medical records of the Nottingham attacks victims.

Nottingham students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, who was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.

In May, Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) NHS Trust confirmed it had dismissed 11 members of staff and, in an update on Friday, said a total of 15 people had now been sacked as part of its investigation.

The families of Barnaby, Grace and Ian previously welcomed the action taken by the trust but called the development in May a "kick in the teeth".

Dr Manjeet Shehmar, medical director at NUH, said: "There is simply no excuse for accessing the records of a patient without a legitimate reason and I hope this sends a really clear message – we will investigate and we will take action.

"To lose a loved one in the way that the families of Ian, Grace and Barnaby have is heartbreaking enough.

"I am so sorry that they have had this further compounded by the actions of these staff members."

As well as the dismissals, NUH said 15 final written warnings and two first written warnings have also been issued in total.

Two cases were found to have no case to answer and no action was taken.

The trust said action had been taken against "doctors, nurses, registered healthcare professionals and other staff" and that independent regulators such as the Nursing and Midwifery Council and General Medical Council, the Information Commissioner's Office, and Nottinghamshire Police had been informed.

A new system, currently under testing, is being implemented to protect patient records in future and alert the trust of potential breaches.

A Your Responsibility, Your Actions, Their Privacy campaign has also been carried out to educate staff about data protection and the "serious consequences" of not following the rules, it added.

Shehmar said: "We will continue to investigate inappropriate access to these records and take action as and where necessary.

"Alongside this, we are doing all we can to educate our staff on appropriate access and how to keep the records of our patients safe. We are also introducing a new system which acts to detect possible data breaches.

"While the actions of these staff members are disappointing, we know that this represents a small number of our wider workforce.

"We know staff across the trust are listening, learning and doing what they can to ensure that only lawful and justified access takes place in our hospitals."

NUH said investigations were continuing, including into inappropriate access of the files of the surviving victims of the attacks - Wayne Birkett, Sharon Miller and Marcin Gawronski.

The first dismissals were made public amid a statutory public inquiry examining the lead-up to the attacks and decisions and actions taken in the aftermath.

The judge-led Nottingham Inquiry heard from 164 witnesses during 14 weeks of harrowing evidence between February and June 2026, as well as two days of closing statements from core participants in September.

The findings of the inquiry, which is being led by retired senior judge Deborah Taylor KC, will be published by May 2027.

The hearings scrutinised authorities that had interactions with Calocane in the years before the attacks, laying bare failures and missed opportunities by agencies, including the NHS and police.

The inquiry heard Calocane had been sectioned four times under the Mental Health Act and had a history of police interactions linked to violent incidents before the killings.

Calocane is serving an indefinite hospital order, after pleading guilty to manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility, due to his paranoid schizophrenia, in January 2024.

NUH is among a number of organisations in which staff inappropriately viewed records or information related to the fatal attacks.

In December 2024, an investigation opened into allegations Ministry of Justice (MoJ) staff illegally accessed computer files related to the Nottingham attacks.

Amy Holmes, the interim director general for the chief operating group of the Ministry of Justice (MoJ), told the inquiry she could not detail what information was accessed due to the ongoing police investigation.

The inquiry also heard seven probation service officers were identified as having accessed the information.

HM Prison and Probation Service found four of those officers accessed files legitimately, but three did not have a legitimate reason to do so.

However, it was deemed by the probation service and the Ministry of Justice's data protection unit that the breaches were not serious enough to warrant further action.

Footage and images related to the attacks were also viewed numerous times by Nottinghamshire Police staff without a legitimate policing purpose.

The force confirmed it would carry out an audit of how many times the information was viewed and whether it was appropriate, following a complaint by Barnaby's mother , Emma Webber, in March.

articles.title: GOP lawmakers bash Trump’s decision to waive Russia sanctions: ‘Beyond irresponsible’
articles.summary: Several GOP lawmakers criticized President Trump’s move to exempt Russia from the sanctions bill he signed law last month, with Sen. Thom Tillis (R- N.C.) calling the move “beyond irresponsible.” Trump signed an executive order Friday evening to waive sanctions against Russia in a legislative package that was meant to put pressure on the Kremlin…
articles.body:
Several GOP lawmakers criticized President Trump’s move to exempt Russia from the sanctions bill he signed law last month, with Sen. Thom Tillis (R- N.C.) calling the move “beyond irresponsible.”

Trump signed an executive order Friday evening to waive sanctions against Russia in a legislative package that was meant to put pressure on the Kremlin to end its military operations against Ukraine.

“What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand? It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day,” Tillis wrote on the social platform X.

The legislation, signed by Trump in September , would impose tariffs on the top five purchasers of Russian energy, or on countries helping Russia evade sanctions.

The sanctions bill was drafted by and named after late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). The late senator had announced a breakthrough on the legislation shortly before his death in July, saying lawmakers reached a deal with the White House to move it forward.

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) posted the news on social media Saturday morning saying, “Lindsey would be appalled.”

“The President is prolonging the war, not ending it,” Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) wrote on social media , referring to Friday’s executive order.

In his Friday order , the president noted that the legislation allows him to “waive the application of any sanctions provision with respect to a foreign person.”

“I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” Trump said in the order. “I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States.”

One the other side of the aisle, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who played a major role in passing the sanctions bill, called the president’s move to waive sanctions for Russia, a “craven, cowardly action.”

“These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, & everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,” Blumenthal wrote in his post.

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) also slammed the president’s move on social platform X , saying it “betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression.”

The move comes after the president struck a deal with Russia last week permitting the country to sell diesel products to the U.S. and in the world market amid global fuel shortages. The deal prompted backlash from lawmakers across the board.

In an interview with Piers Morgan, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he felt “betrayed” by the president’s decision.

articles.summary: Indian Captain Smit Machchhar, who survived an assault by his Omani co-pilot aboard a flydubai flight in September, recalled the ordeal and how he might
articles.body: Indian Captain Smit Machchhar, who survived an assault by his Omani co-pilot aboard a flydubai flight in September, recalled the ordeal and how he might not survive.In a teaser released by Sky News Arabia ahead of an exclusive interview, asked whether there was a moment when he thought he might not make it, Machchhar said he told himself he needed to act before it was too late. "I mean, I'm trying to get over it now, but yes, there was a moment that I realised, and I told myself that, Smith, do something. You can't die like this," he said."I'm not saying I accepted my death. It was like, do something, otherwise..." he added, describing the moment when he realised that he had to act.Machchhar also recalled the scene after the cockpit door was opened, describing the panic and screaming. "I remember being face down, and of course the panic which was there, the screaming which was there," he said.He also praised the colleague who took over the controls during the crisis, calling the colleague's actions commendable. "It's something that I'll keep with me till I die," Machchhar said.The interview comes weeks after the September 30 incident aboard flydubai flight FZ1073, which was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The Indian captain was allegedly attacked by his Omani co-pilot, identified as Hamam al-Hammami, inside the cockpit.Despite his injuries, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to intervene and overpower the alleged attacker. articles.title: Albanian anti-government protesters clash with police in Tirana
articles.summary: Thousands of young Albanians gathered outside the Education Ministry in ​the center of the capital Tirana on Saturday on the fifth day of a growing student-led movement ‌to force Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
articles.body: Thousands of young Albanians gathered outside the Education Ministry in ​the center of the capital Tirana on Saturday on the fifth day of a growing student-led movement ‌to force Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. The protest turned violent when a group of young people wearing masks hurled rocks at riot police, who responded with stun grenades, tear gas and a water cannon. Demonstrations over corruption and a lack ​of jobs have begun spreading throughout Albania. In Tirana this week, protesters smashed windows, set alight ​government buildings and clashed with police. Police figures showed that 500 protesters had been detained ⁠so far, 330 of whom were released. Some 120 police and 45 protesters were registered as injured, ​although many injuries to protesters are likely to have gone unrecorded. The unrest is emerging as the biggest threat ​to Rama, who has governed since 2013 and won a fourth term in elections last year. It follows months of largely peaceful protests triggered by plans to build a luxury resort on Albania’s pristine southern coastline, backed by investors including US President Donald Trump’s ​son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Villagers told Reuters in July that their land had been wrongfully sold for the development. ​Reuters later reported that the man who sold the land was wanted by prosecutors on suspicion of drug trafficking, accusations ‌his ⁠lawyer denied. Reuters found no evidence of wrongdoing by Kushner, who is not directly involved in the villagers’ dispute. Rama’s administration has been dogged by corruption scandals and analysts say Albania is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking, complicating its efforts to join the EU. Rama, who denies wrongdoing and this ​week told Reuters that ​he would not step ⁠down, said on Saturday that his government respected the students and would protect their right to protest. “My responsibility is even clearer during these difficult times ... to protect ​our citizens, guarantee justice, and move Albania forward — together with this governing majority, ​which holds ⁠a very clear mandate: to see Albania in the European Union by 2030,” he said on Facebook. Along with Montenegro, Albania is leading the accession process among Balkan countries. Albania’s unrest coincides with growing street protests elsewhere in Europe. In ⁠France, high-school ​students have been protesting for weeks to demand more teachers and better ​facilities, a campaign that looks to be spreading to other population groups. Spain this month experienced broad protests against high rents and a ​lack of housing, which prompted the government to call a snap election.

articles.title: Coronavirus has destroyed the institution of marriage; Covid time matrimonial disputes must be dealt  with separately: Madras high court
articles.summary: CHENNAI: Coronavirus has not only taken away human lives but has also destroyed the institution of marriage, the Madras high court has said.
articles.body: CHENNAI: Coronavirus has not only taken away human lives but has also destroyed the institution of marriage, the Madras high court has said. “Since the couples were inside the same house, the best and worst aspects of their characters were exposed and most of them were under pressure, thinking about their future and it had a direct impact on their marital relationship,” the court added.Therefore, those matrimonial disputes that arose during this period -- 2020 to 2022 -- must be dealt with as a separate category and out of box thinking is required to resolve these disputes, Justice N Anand Venkatesh said. The court then directed district judges in Tamil Nadu to collect data from family courts dealing with matrimonial disputes pertaining to those marriages which had taken place between 2020 to 2022.“If the data is placed before this court before the next date of hearing, this court will seek the assistance of counsel who has rich experience in family court disputes and see if a different kind of solution can be adopted in all these cases,” the judge said.“This court is confident that such a step will surely have a positive impact, and it will help many families coming together by resolving the dispute amicably,” the court, adjourning the hearing to Nov 27 for filing the report.Justice Anand Venkatesh passed the order while confirming an order passed by a family court directing a husband to pay Rs 10,000 as an interim maintenance to his wife pending adjudication of their matrimonial dispute. “Before drawing the curtains in the present case, this court has noticed that, in the last three months, in almost every matrimonial dispute that has reached this court, the marriages had taken place between the parties between 2019 to 2022,” he said.In more than 95% of those cases, the parties had hardly lived together for six to nine months and in some cases, they had lived together only for three months. articles.title: A proposed A$15 billion data-centre campus near Wagga Wagga would use about 100 hectares, 384 backup generators and 6,400 tonnes of diesel; more than 1,000 residents have signed a petition against it
articles.summary: A proposed A$15 billion data-centre campus near Wagga Wagga in New South Wales has sparked a debate over the future of regional development, with
articles.body: A proposed A$15 billion data-centre campus near Wagga Wagga in New South Wales has sparked a debate over the future of regional development, with residents raising concerns about agricultural land, energy demand and environmental impacts. Reporting by ABC Riverina and The Daily Telegraph, alongside details in the project’s planning documents, highlights a growing divide between those concerned about the development and those who see it as a major economic opportunity. CDC Data Centres is exploring plans for a 1.4-gigawatt facility on approximately 100 hectares of council-owned land at Gregadoo, around 15 kilometres from central Wagga Wagga. The proposed campus would comprise four large, single-storey buildings designed to operate around the clock.The scale of the project has drawn particular attention. Its proposed infrastructure includes 384 backup diesel generators, diesel storage estimated at 6,400 tonnes, large-scale batteries and substantial electricity connections. If built, the campus would represent a significant addition to Australia’s expanding data-centre industry, which is being driven in part by growing demand for cloud computing and artificial intelligence. More than 1,000 people have signed a petition opposing the proposal, calling on Wagga Wagga City Council, the NSW Government and relevant planning authorities to reject the development.Concerns over farmland and local impactsThe proposed site is currently zoned for primary production, meaning a change in land-use zoning would be required to accommodate the development. Because the project is classified as a State Significant Development, the approval decision would be made at the state level rather than by the local council. Residents living near Gregadoo have questioned whether the potential economic gains would justify the project’s impact on the surrounding rural landscape. Concerns include the effect on neighbouring homes, farming activities, noise, emissions and the long-term industrialisation of agricultural land. The proposed energy demand is another central issue. CDC estimates that the completed campus could consume between five and seven terawatt-hours of electricity annually, depending on customer requirements and operating capacity. The company expects the facility to run at around 40 to 60 per cent of its maximum capacity. The proposal also includes approximately 20,160 rooftop solar panels, expected to generate up to 13.1 megawatts under peak conditions. However, this would account for only a small fraction of the campus’s proposed 1.4-gigawatt maximum capacity.Water use and environmental questionsWater consumption has emerged as another point of discussion, particularly in a region where residents are concerned about changing climatic conditions and pressure on natural resources. CDC has said it intends to use a closed-loop cooling system that recirculates water rather than relying on conventional evaporative cooling methods. The company estimates annual water consumption during the initial stage at approximately 1.512 million litres, with an initial fill of around 1.28 million litres also anticipated. The developer has indicated that the initial water requirement could be met through rainwater collected on-site, supplemented by water deliveries or town supplies depending on local conditions. Its broader proposal also includes funding connections and upgrades to infrastructure that the site currently lacks, including water, sewerage and telecommunications services. Despite these assurances, residents and sustainability specialists have called for more detailed information about the project’s environmental footprint and long-term resource requirements. A comprehensive assessment is expected to address issues including electricity infrastructure, noise and vibration, water management and other potential environmental impacts.Economic opportunities versus community concernsSupporters argue that a development of this scale could bring substantial investment to the region. Wagga Wagga City Council has described the proposal as a potentially significant opportunity for the local economy, pointing to construction activity, contracts for local suppliers, skilled employment and training opportunities. CDC has also indicated that the project could generate hundreds of jobs during construction, alongside ongoing employment once operational. The extent of these benefits, however, will depend on the final design, construction schedule and staffing requirements.The proposal has also prompted questions about whether establishing major digital infrastructure could encourage further data-centre developments in the area. Researchers examining sustainable digital infrastructure have warned that such projects can make surrounding regions more attractive to other operators, potentially increasing pressure on agricultural land and existing infrastructure. For local business and community representatives, the challenge is to assess the proposal on its merits while ensuring that residents have a meaningful role in the process.What happens next?The project remains subject to assessment under New South Wales’ State Significant Development process. Although Wagga Wagga City Council has endorsed the sale of the land, the state government will determine whether the data-centre campus can proceed.CDC has proposed a community benefits package worth up to A$225 million, comprising a contribution linked to the development’s estimated cost and a further A$75 million for local initiatives. Potential priorities include housing, sporting facilities, education, environmental improvements and community infrastructure. The commitments are conditional on the project receiving approval and proceeding as planned. The debate now centres on whether the promised economic and community benefits will outweigh concerns about energy demand, diesel storage, agricultural land and the long-term environmental consequences of a development of this scale.You use AI every day. articles.title: Hurricane Trudy makes its way toward Mexico as Typhoon Champi threatens Guam
articles.summary: Hurricane Trudy moved toward southwestern and west-central areas of Mexico’s Pacific coast and could keep growing through Saturday, forecasters said.
articles.body: Hurricane Trudy moved toward southwestern and west-central areas of Mexico’s Pacific coast and could keep growing through Saturday, forecasters said. The center of Trudy will approach the coast on Saturday and pass near it into Sunday. A hurricane warning was in effect from Manzanillo in Colima state to Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco. The storm was a Category 1 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 90 mph on Friday night. Trudy was about 240 miles west-southwest of Acapulco, in the Mexican state of Guerrero, and about 215 miles south-southeast of Manzanillo, Colima state, while moving northwest at 8 mph, the U.S. National Hurricane Center said. The Mexican navy urged the maritime community and coastal residents to exercise extreme caution due to high waves, heavy rains and the risk of rising river levels, flooding and landslides in vulnerable areas. The state of Colima has said that risks are currently low, but the storm could bring significant rainfall that could have damaging effects due to the saturated ground following the successive storms that have hit the Pacific coast. Through the weekend, Trudy is expected to produce 4 to 8 inches of rain, with isolated higher totals around 15 inches. Also in the Pacific, Typhoon Champi became a major category 4 storm as it moved west toward Guam at 15 mph. Maximum sustained winds were 130 mph, according to the U.S. Weather Service. Forecasters said it could become a super typhoon in the next 12 hours. It was forecast to pass just south of Guam. A typhoon warning was issued for Guam and Rota along with a tropical storm warning for Tinian, Saipan and nearby areas.

articles.title: California residents are waking up to their homes sliding into the ocean. And the worst is yet to come.
articles.summary: The worst of El Niño is still months away, but Southern California’s fragile coastline is already being transformed by record-setting king tides and storm surges.
articles.body: LONG BEACH, Calif. — It was 3:30 a.m. on Oct. 9 and the unthinkable was happening all around Shawn Curtis: The boardwalk in front of his two-story beachfront apartment building was gone. The 25-foot-wide sand beach was gone. Salt water poured in from all sides. And now the building was slanting down into the ocean. Curtis couldn’t make sense of what he saw. “The doorframe was crooked. The window was crooked, and then I saw a big wave crash,” he told NBC News on Thursday. The surf crashed all the way up to the second floor. Neighbors across the street said they could see water cascading down onto the roof of Curtis’ home of nine years. Booming waves were loud enough to wake him and shake his apartment as though an earthquake rippled through, he said. “We rushed for our lives, but it was clear the house was toast,” Curtis said, referring to his roommate. “It was a foregone conclusion. It was gone.” The worst of El Niño is still months away, but Southern California’s fragile coastline is already being transformed by record-setting king tides and storm surges. An unusually active hurricane season triggered a trio of storms that pummeled Hawaii and Mexico earlier this year. The historic weather pattern claimed more than a dozen homes along the shore in Long Beach, swallowing up boardwalks and portions of the Pacific Coast Highway farther south. “This is just a little bit of a taste of what we will see in the future,” warned Timu Gallien with the Coastal Flood Lab at the University of California, Los Angeles. Last weekend, destructive surf thrashed coastal communities from Malibu to San Diego, flooding neighborhoods in Newport Beach and forcing people to evacuate homes in Long Beach that were once protected by wide sand beaches and reinforced boardwalks. The devastation spread on a sunny, calm weekend without warning. California did not experience any rain or wind before massive swells overtook Laguna Beach, where a portion of the PCH remains closed as sections crack and slide down toward the ocean. “People don’t realize there was a beach here,” Long Beach Peninsula resident Dana Marie Lazzareschi said Thursday. “These houses aren’t on the water.” Paradise lost Lazzareschi said she fell in love with the peninsula’s diversity and sense of community when she first moved into her rental four years ago. Neighbors were chatty and looked out for each other. They walked their dogs, rode bicycles up and down the street and were quick to help if someone needed it. But on Oct. 9, as she watched waves splash onto rooftops, she wondered how long she could stay. “I definitely wouldn’t buy a home here now,” she said. “But it really is such a dream.” For decades, scientists and marine biologists have warned that increasing global temperatures would trigger rising sea levels and inevitably lead to more coastal flooding. This year, those existing factors coincide with what is predicted to become the strongest El Niño event in recorded history. El Niño is a natural climate pattern associated with intense rainfall and storms in the Southeast and warm conditions in the Pacific Northwest that can cause strong, dangerous surf. But it doesn’t end there. Kelvin waves, which travel hundreds of miles underwater, can cause waves to rise another foot. Alone, Kelvin waves generally don’t lead to coastal flooding, but when paired with high tides that exceed 7 feet and storm surges on top of that, the combination can be catastrophic, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. “Although the waves and the tide levels are receding slightly right now, very slightly, there still is ongoing coastal flooding, and this is not really going to get any better for months,” said climate scientist Daniel Swain. “In fact, it’s likely to get worse before it gets better,” he said, adding that Northern California will begin to experience similar behavior in November and December. Coastal communities in Southern California began to experience dangerous conditions over Labor Day weekend with the remnants of Hurricane Marie. That was followed soon after by remnants of Hurricane Polo at the end of September and now Tropical Storm Rachel. The peak of a historic El Niño is expected to hit early next year, but three more rounds of seasonal high tides this year will likely bring more flooding and erosion, said Gallien, who is also an associate professor of environmental and civil engineering at UCLA. “It’s a lot of water pointed at our coast,” she said. ‘Not built for this’ Two weeks before losing his home, Curtis told his landlord he wanted to move out, he said. Seven-foot waves triggered by hurricanes Marie and Polo had already eaten away at the boardwalk in front of his apartment and he worried that the damage would only worsen with the incoming El Niño that is expected to peak in January and February. Using wooden planks and sandbags, Long Beach City work crews earlier this month had patched up holes in the boardwalk’s wall created by the hurricanes, but the reinforcements did not hold. Mayor Rex Richardson told reporters last week that the city’s “infrastructure was not built for this” and said repairs will continue during the lower tides. But residents and experts are questioning how much longer coastal living will be possible with rapid climate change. “We love to live in these vulnerable places because they are beautiful,” Gallien said. “It comes down to what is a risk tolerance for a given homeowner or a given community, or a given municipality. Can engineers protect structures?” This is one of the biggest questions keeping officials, residents and experts up at night. While the ongoing damage to California’s coastline is historic in nature, it is not necessarily unprecedented. Coastal erosion has caused flooding along the PCH during previous El Niños, including in the mid-1980s and late 1990s. On the Long Beach Peninsula, more than a dozen homes crumbled into the ocean between Oct. 9 and 11 when the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel stirred offshore waves up to 17 feet tall. Eight structures encompassing 13 homes were deemed too unsafe to enter. Curtis said he loved waking up to the soothing sound of surf every morning. His front door opened onto a popular boardwalk filled with locals and visitors taking in the stunning views. When his apartment began to collapse, Curtis said he and his roommate rushed to shove whatever they could toward the back of the building and into the garage, which remained dry and felt more stable. He escaped by climbing through his bedroom window with his dog Lux and went to the other side of the street, which faces the bay and evaded damage this time. A few days later, friends showed Curtis drone footage of his favorite couch floating in the ocean. “It’s just a couch,” he said. “I feel really bad for the neighbors.” Next door, a three-floor single-family home remained empty this week. Its owners, a family of three, left for a cruise before the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel destroyed their property. A giant crack snaked from the foundation up to the roof, threatening to split the house in two. Curtis said he told them just to enjoy their vacation. There was nothing they could do. The family could not be reached for comment. On Thursday, Curtis’ roommate, who did not want to be named, rushed to shove what few belongings he saved into a U-Haul truck as inspectors and contractors looked on. Tenants had two hours to retrieve what they could before crews would begin the dangerous process of tearing down the building, the roommates said. Down the block, Curtis walked around his neighborhood with the unmistakable countenance of someone who had just survived a disaster. He’d been wearing the same clothes for a few days and couldn’t remember the date. Days had blurred together into a whirlwind of phone calls and emails to his landlord, city officials, family and insurance. When asked whether he would consider leaving the peninsula, he did not hesitate. “Not a chance,” he said. “But I am moving to the other side.

articles.title: 7,000-year-old bones uncovered at construction site in startling find
articles.summary: A 7,000-year-old skeleton from the Linear Pottery culture was found in Leipzig, Germany, during a school construction dig, marking the city's oldest grave.
articles.body: Archaeologists excavating the site of a planned elementary school in Germany have unearthed a roughly 7,000-year-old skeleton — the oldest known grave ever discovered in the city. The discovery, made in the German city of Leipzig, was announced by the Saxony State Office for Archaeology in late September. Archaeologists were brought in ahead of the school's construction because the site was near a previously known Bronze Age archaeological site, officials said in a statement. ANCIENT 'SEATED' SKELETONS UNEARTHED BENEATH MODERN SCHOOL SITE, PUZZLING ARCHAEOLOGISTS "Prehistoric finds were also to be expected simply because of the site's flood-free location near the White Elster River, within the fertile Leipzig Lowland Basin, an area exceptionally rich in archaeological finds," they added. Instead of simple artifacts, the excavation uncovered the remains of an ancient Neolithic settlement, including the roughly 7,000-year-old grave. The grave dates to a period when people were transitioning from hunting and gathering to living in permanent settlements, farming and raising livestock, according to officials. The person buried there is believed to have belonged to the Linear Pottery culture — named for the distinctive spiral and wavy patterns decorating its pottery. SHOCKING DISCOVERY OF ANCIENT BONES TURNS COUPLE'S KITCHEN RENOVATION INTO 'CRIME SCENE' Archaeologists also uncovered the remains of a 98-foot-long wooden house, along with evidence of at least two other houses. "The discovery of a burial within the settlement came as a surprise." The experts were taken aback by the unexpected discovery of the grave. "The discovery of a burial within the settlement came as a surprise," officials said. "This is a rare stroke of luck because, in large parts of Saxony, bone preservation is so poor that graves can only be identified by the objects placed in them and the shapes of the burial pits." DISCOVERY BENEATH SOCCER FIELD REVEALS MASSIVE MEDIEVAL CONVENT LOST FOR CENTURIES Although officials have not identified the person's sex or age at death, they said the skeleton was found lying on its left side, with its legs drawn up. The grave contained no grave goods — objects buried alongside the dead — but archaeologists were able to estimate its age based on the skeleton's crouched position and the grave's relationship to the nearby settlement and one of its houses. "In this case, the crouched position of the body, together with the grave's direct stratigraphic relationship to the settlement and one of its houses, makes it possible to date the burial to the Neolithic Linear Pottery culture, even in the absence of grave goods," the statement said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Officials added, "This means that the approximately 7,000-year-old burial is the oldest grave discovered to date within the city limits of Leipzig." Archaeologists will continue excavating the site until the middle of this month, when the Saxony State Office for Archaeology is expected to begin its scientific analysis. State archaeologist Regina Smolnik emphasized the importance of conducting archaeological investigations even in heavily developed areas. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "Our investigations in Leipzig-Möckern demonstrate very clearly how important the involvement of archaeology is, even in urban areas," Smolnik said in a statement. "Although such sites have long since become part of the urban landscape and have been built over for many years, important evidence of prehistoric and early historic settlement can still be documented there." Last year, archaeologists in Poland uncovered an 11th-century grave that had been reopened more than 1,000 years ago, apparently by people living during the medieval period. articles.title: Man calls for PM Andy Burnham to intervene after wife detained in Egypt
articles.summary: Eman el-Shazly has been held by authorities in Egypt for two months, allegedly due to her sister's activism.
articles.body:
The husband of a woman who was detained by the Egyptian authorities has called for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to get involved and help with her release.

Eman el-Shazly, from Handsworth Wood, in Birmingham, was taken from her mother's house in Cairo two months ago, allegedly in relation to her sister's online activism.

Her husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, said that their family felt "very helpless" and that their "only possible solution" was for Burnham to "make a phone call to Egypt" to end the detainment.

The BBC has approached the Egyptian consulate in London for a response. The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said it was in contact with authorities in Egypt.

Moustapha said he had had "no contact whatsoever" with his wife, but had heard from her mother that her health had deteriorated due to a lack of food and medical assistance.

"It's not a five-star hotel, there's 30 individuals sleeping in a cell with one toilet and one shower," he said.

He told the BBC that his wife had travelled to Egypt to look after her elderly, sick mother, who had been undertaking 18-hour round trips to take food to el-Shazly's two brothers in detention.

The 46-year-old claimed his wife had been detained due to her sister's online posts from the UK targeting the Egyptian leadership

"How somebody can make videos abroad knowing it's causing direct consequences to people abroad, what kind of person can sleep at night doing that," he said.

Her sister told the BBC that she was sorry that her family had been detained. She said this was a tactic used by the Egyptian government to silence critics.

But she would not stop posting her videos, because she felt it was her duty to make a stand.

Moustapha described support from the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) as "useless" with no calls or updates from them.

"We are very angry, we feel that the government isn't doing anything to secure the release of a British citizen," he said, adding that his wife had held a British passport for 20 years.

Moustapha, who has four children, said there was no evidence against his wife, who was being left "to rot in jail" and that it was a "clear example of collective punishment".

"The kids are very distraught, they are suffering, they've lost their mother at the moment and we genuinely don't know what to do about it," he said.

A spokesperson for the FCDO said: "We are supporting the family of a British national detained in Egypt, and are in contact with the authorities."

articles.title: Zelensky on Trump waiving Russia sanctions: ‘This Act could have helped enormously’
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky decried President Trump’s late-night decision to waive sanctions and tariffs against Russia days before they were set to take effect under a new law. “At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard…
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky decried President Trump’s late-night decision to waive sanctions and tariffs against Russia days before they were set to take effect under a new law.

“At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end,” Zelensky wrote in Saturday morning statement posted to social platform X .

“This Act could have helped enormously – and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters,” the Ukrainian leader continued.

The sweeping legislative sanctions package , which was named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), would have raised tariffs up to 100 percent on goods imported to the U.S. from the five largest purchasers of Russian fuel amid the country’s yearslong war against Ukraine. Trump signed the package into law last month.

On Friday night, the president issued an executive order that waived this sanction package, saying it was “in the national interests of the United States.” This followed his decision last week to ease sanctions on Russian oil, permitting the country to “immediately” begin selling 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and global markets.

These relief measures come amid rising fuel costs in the U.S. and abroad brought on by the Iran war, which have placed pressure on the Trump administration to address Americans’ affordability concerns ahead of the midterm elections.

Ukraine and Russia have targeted each other’s energy infrastructure in recent military operations. Zelensky reported Saturday that Russia had “scaled up” these attacks, launching over 320 attack drones against Ukraine’s energy sector in a 12-hour period starting yesterday evening.

The Ukrainian leader accused the Russian government of “trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine” before the winter season.

“Pressure is needed to stop this,” he said in his Saturday statement. “A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. “

Zelensky added, “We must not give up ground. We must keep trying to end the war. To end it, not give Putin every reason to continue it indefinitely. I thank everyone who is truly fighting for peace and helping Ukraine!”

articles.title: Low-cost RSPCA clinic in Chatham helps pet owners with vet bills
articles.summary: RSPCA Medway West launches its clinic for the pets of people with low incomes.
articles.body:
A reduced-cost veterinary clinic has treated 160 pets in its first 11 days, according to the RSPCA.

The animal charity's Medway West branch has launched to offer cut-price care for the pets of people on low incomes or receiving benefits.

"Your pet would come first. You'd have a bit of toast yourself and pay out for your pet," said Chatham cat owner Christine Gardner. "Having somewhere like this is amazing."

She told the BBC it was "just really good to have something nearby that I can get to" with her six cats.

Angela Adams said her pets were her "babies", adding: "I would rather starve than they starve."

She said she had eight cats, two rabbits, four guinea pigs, two African land snails and a tortoise, and that she did not know what she would do without the animals, as she was unable to work for health reasons.

"It's very expensive. Seven of my cats were due for vaccine this month and you can imagine the cost of that," she told the BBC. "That's a lot of money."

"I've had friends messaging me struggling, so this place is brilliant for people."

RSPCA branch account manager Imara Ó Niocail said that "a lot of people who were more than capable of affording to have these animals" were no longer able to care for them due to the cost of living or a change in circumstances.

"We would like to keep the animals at home with the owners and treat them there," Ó Niocail told the BBC.

The low cost clinic meant that pet owners in Medway could "seek the treatment that they need and then take the animals home", without having to pay the full vet costs , she added.

Medway West branch manager Kevin Morton said the charity's centres were "full-to-bursting" with animals and some people "give their animals up because they can't afford to look after them".

"Some people might think that if you can't afford to feed it, then don't have it, but if it's your only companion you have, they can keep people going," he said.

The branch has supplied 18,909 food items, 1,294 treats and 919kg of biscuits so far in 2026 through its pet food bank.

articles.title: Hurricane Trudy makes its way towards Mexico, threatening heavy rain
articles.summary: Trudy is the latest in successive storms that have hit Mexico’s Pacific coast this year.
articles.body:
Hurricane Trudy ‌maintained its strength as it moved towards Mexico’s western ⁠coast on ⁠Saturday, with forecasters warning it could strengthen further before beginning to weaken on Sunday.

A hurricane warning was in effect from Manzanillo in Colima state to Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco.

The United States National Hurricane Center said ⁠Trudy was about 305km (190 miles) south-southeast of Manzanillo early on Saturday, with maximum sustained winds of 150 km/h (90mph).

The hurricane was moving at about 13km/h (8mph) and was forecast to approach southwestern and west-central Mexico later on Saturday before passing near the coast overnight into Sunday.

Hurricane conditions are expected ‌in the warning area on Saturday night, while tropical storm conditions are expected to spread across the region during the day, the NHC said. Hurricane conditions are also possible in areas under a hurricane watch.

Trudy is forecast to bring 10 to 20cm (four to eight inches) of rain, ⁠with isolated totals of about 38cm (15 ⁠inches), across parts of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco through the weekend, raising the risk of life-threatening flooding and landslides, especially in steep terrain, according to the NHC.

Outer ⁠rain bands could produce two to four inches of rain, with isolated totals of ⁠approximately 15cm (six inches), in Guerrero and Nayarit, ⁠where localised flash flooding is possible, the centre said.

The NHC also warned of possible coastal flooding from storm surge in areas exposed to onshore winds, accompanied ‌by large and destructive waves.

Swells generated by Trudy were already affecting parts of Mexico’s southwestern coast and are expected to spread ‌northward towards ‌the country’s west-central coast through the weekend, creating life-threatening surf and rip current conditions, the NHC said.

The Mexican navy urged the maritime community and coastal residents to exercise extreme caution due to high waves, heavy rains and the risk of rising river levels, flooding and landslides in vulnerable areas.

The state of Colima has said that risks are currently low, but the storm could bring significant rainfall that could have damaging effects due to the saturated ground following the successive storms that have hit the Pacific coast.

articles.title: Why adults are going back to summer camp
articles.summary: Loneliness and burnout are sending adults around the world back to bunk beds and bonfires.
articles.body:
After dinner, the marshmallows came out. A group of nurses and support staff from a New York City clinic gathered around the campfire, sharing stories about childhood and how they got into the field. Above them, the upstate New York sky was full of stars. For a few hours in July 2026, the clinical titles and workplace hierarchies that normally defined this group of US health professionals disappeared.

Aleksey Aronov, CEO of VIP's IV, had brought his team to Camp No Counselors for a four-day weekend to unwind and bond.

“A lot of my staff members were new, and some were quite shy,” Aronov said. “But after the camp experience, everyone felt comfortable around one another, got to know each other better and bonded seamlessly.”

His team had arrived together. Other campers go looking for a group to belong to.

For adults heading to summer camp, the draw goes beyond childhood memories. Some are turning to camp experiences to network or mitigate burnout, while others are seeking a way to make new friends. Whatever their reason, an increasing number of people around the world are finding that the summer camps of their youth are the perfect antidote to the pressures of modern adult life.

Mia Morin, 29, of Toronto and her husband attended YMCA Camp Queen Elizabeth on Beausoleil Island in Ontario, Canada in May 2025 to meet new people.

“We wanted to gather around interesting people, exchange ideas and do things together,” Morin says. “Going to YMCA Camp Queen Elizabeth was easy because nobody there was random. Since everyone has already selected the same thing, you have a starting point with something in common.”

Once a niche getaway for nostalgic campers, adult camps have exploded in popularity, offering weekend and weeklong retreats where grown-ups trade screen time and their comfy beds for campfires, sports, arts and crafts, and bunk beds. Unlike the children’s day and overnight camps, however, today’s adult versions often include grown-up perks, such as open bars, wine tastings, chef-prepared meals and wellness programming.

Yelp’s 2025 Trend Forecast showed searches for “adult camps” were up 347 percent from September 2023 through August 2024, compared with the previous 12-month period. The online directory of the American Camp Association (ACA) lists 85 adult camp programmes in the United States, and while the ACA does not track the number of adult camps year-over-year, it confirms that there has been positive growth in adult camp programming over the last decade.

As of 2026, the concept has expanded well beyond the US and Canada, with camps launching in destinations ranging from the Swiss Alps to the United Arab Emirates.

“The rising popularity of adult camps reflects a larger movement toward meaningful, in-person experiences we’ve been seeing through Yelp,” said Yelp’s trend expert, Tara Lewis.

“People are looking to unplug and foster connections in shared physical spaces. These camps give adults the chance to go analog, rediscover favourite activities, focus on wellness and make genuine connections," she added.

Just how much has the concept grown? When founder Adam Tichauer pitched Camp No Counselors to the reality TV contest Shark Tank in 2016, the sharks didn’t bite. Fast forward 10 years, and all the Camp No Counselors dates through 2027 have waitlists.

articles.title: Unauthorised wiring blamed for PGVCL worker’s death
articles.summary: PGVCL worker died of electrocution in Rajkot; police booked industrial unit owner after probe found unauthorised wiring possibly energised a shut feeder.
articles.body: Rajkot: Kotda Sangani police have registered a case against the owner of an industrial unit after a PGVCL worker died of electrocution while carrying out maintenance work in Rampara village of Rajkot district on Oct 1.The case was filed under Section 105 of the BNS against Gordhan Ramani, owner of Nyal Karan Industries, following a complaint by Paschim Gujarat Vij Company Ltd (PGVCL). The power utility’s preliminary inquiry allegedly found an unauthorised electrical arrangement that may have allowed electricity from a Jyotigram feeder to flow into an agricultural feeder.The deceased, Lalsingh Palas, was working on a transformer connected to an agricultural feeder that had been shut down for maintenance. While installing a drop-out (DO) fuse after the transformer was replaced, he allegedly received an electric shock when power unexpectedly resumed on the agricultural line.According to the complaint, a contractor authorised by PGVCL had been replacing a burnt 10KVA transformer serving an agricultural connection in the village. The contractor’s team obtained line clearance from the 66KV Ramod substation before beginning the work.After the transformer replacement, Palas and a colleague started fitting the DO fuse. During the process, electricity allegedly flowed into the feeder, electrocuting Palas and causing him to suffer fatal injuries. He was taken to govt hospital in Kotda Sangani, where he was declared dead.Following the incident, PGVCL officials conducted an inquiry to determine how power reached the agricultural feeder despite its scheduled shutdown. Investigators allegedly found that the 11KV Ramod Jyotigram feeder had been switched on shortly before the accident.During inspections of nearby installations, officials allegedly detected unauthorised wiring at Nyal Karan Industries on Ramod Road. The complaint states that wires connected to a changeover switch at the industrial unit were linked to an agricultural electricity connection reportedly registered in Ramani’s name, creating a possible route for electricity to flow from the industrial line to the agricultural feeder.Deputy engineer Deepakkumar Dhranga filed the complaint on Oct 16, seeking action against Ramani and any other persons found responsible during the investigation.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Rajkot | Silver Rate in Rajkot | Bank Holidays in Rajkot | Public Holidays in Rajkot | Rajkot AQI | Weather in Rajkot | Petrol Price in Rajkot | Diesel Price in Rajkot | CNG Price in Rajkot | LPG Price in RajkotStay updated with the latest Rajkot news. articles.title: Thousands rally for biggest protest in years against Tunisia’s Saied
articles.summary: Unions, opposition groups unite to demonstrate against poor living conditions and restrictions on political freedoms.
articles.body:
Thousands of Tunisians have marched through the capital to protest against President Kais Saied, worsening living conditions and restrictions on political freedoms.

The latest demonstration in Tunis on Saturday was led by the Tunisian General Labour Union (UGTT), an influential trade union federation, alongside opposition parties and civil society organisations.

It was the largest protest against Saied in years, bringing together political opponents whose longstanding divisions have weakened their ability to challenge his rule.

The AFP news agency reported that more than 3,000 people were on the march, but the total could not be independently confirmed.

Protesters gathered along Habib Bourguiba Avenue, a major street in central Tunis, as hundreds of police deployed across the capital. Several surrounding roads were closed.

The crowd included lawyers, doctors, journalists and the unemployed, as well as activists and members of parties from across the political spectrum. They demanded the release of detained government critics and an end to restrictions on trade union rights.

Placards reading “No democracy without freedoms” and “No dignity with poverty” reflected the political and economic grievances driving the demonstration.

Protesters also revived a slogan demanding the government’s removal, widely heard during Tunisia’s 2011 uprising.

Addressing the rally on Saturday, UGTT leader Salah Eddine Salmi criticised the concentration of political power in the presidency and said “silence will no longer be acceptable”.

The political demands came alongside mounting frustration over the cost of basic goods and declining purchasing power.

Tunisia has struggled with prolonged economic difficulties, deteriorating public services, recurring water and electricity cuts, as well as shortages of medicines and other essentials.

Demonstrator Yassine Gharseli, who travelled from Sfax, about 250km south of Tunis, said repeated disruptions to basic services had deepened his frustration with the authorities.

“I came from Sfax to stand up for my freedom,” he told the Reuters news agency at the demo, expressing his determination to continue speaking out.

Saturday’s march followed other demonstrations over similar grievances.

On August 20 , protesters in Tunis rallied against rising prices and shortages of basic goods.

Last month, fuel transport workers went on a two-day strike over wages and working conditions, led by a union federation affiliated with the UGTT.

The demands recall the uprising that ousted longtime President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali in 2011, which helped ignite protests across the Arab world.

Tunisia subsequently held competitive elections and expanded political freedoms, but unemployment and struggling public services remain persistent sources of anger.

Saied came to power promising an alternative to that political system; however, in 2021, he suspended parliament and dismissed the government, saying he was confronting corruption and political deadlock.

He later dissolved parliament and a new constitution increased presidential powers in 2022.

articles.title: Pandal hopping, selfies and street food add sparkle to Saptami
articles.summary: Ranchi Maha Saptami: crowds throng Durga Puja pandals for themed decor, selfies and street food; rain leaves muddy, waterlogged lanes but spirit stays high.
articles.body: Ranchi: New clothes, selfie sessions, street food stops and the thrill of discovering creatively themed pandals turned Maha Saptami into a memorable celebration for revellers across the city on Saturday.From families stepping out after lunch to groups of youngsters planning their pandal-hopping routes, Ranchi remained immersed in the festive spirit. For many, the joy lay as much in the journey as in the destination.“We never decide how many pandals we will visit. We start with one, meet friends at another, stop for chaat somewhere and suddenly realise it is midnight,” said Arav Yadav at Bakri Bazar.The city’s pandals drew large crowds with elaborate decorations, colourful themes and dazzling illuminations. Mobile phones remained busy as visitors captured family portraits, group selfies and social media reels. Children, meanwhile, marvelled at towering idols and the vibrant displays.“Durga Puja is our annual family outing. Everyone gets ready, we eat together and visit pandals we have been coming to since childhood. It brings back so many memories,” said Riddhi, a Harmu resident.Food stalls added to the festive buzz, with visitors pausing between pandal visits for chaat, momos, dosas, bhelpuri and other favourites.“We come for the pandals, but the food makes the evening even better,” said Roma Mahato at Ratu Road.Friday’s heavy rain, however, left several stretches muddy and waterlogged, causing inconvenience to visitors. In Ashok Nagar, resident Dipendar Kumar said several lanes remained submerged after the downpour.The disruption did little to dampen the festive mood. Dressed in bright attire, revellers exchanged greetings, clicked pictures and continued making plans for the next stop in the trail, keeping Ranchi’s streets lively well into the night.Stay updated with the latest Ranchi news. articles.title: Scuffles and fires break out as protesters rally across France, joining students
articles.summary: A car and a newspaper kiosk were set on fire in Paris as police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse violent groups of protesters, while similar tensions erupted in other big cities on the fringes of nationwide demonstrations against rising living costs and in support of high school students’ grievances.
articles.body: PARIS — A car and a newspaper kiosk were set on fire in Paris as police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse violent groups of protesters, while similar tensions erupted in other big cities on the fringes of nationwide demonstrations against rising living costs and in support of high school students’ grievances. In Lyon, France’s third-largest city, fire broke out inside a tourist office. Smoke and flames were seen rising from the building. In the southern port city of Marseille, some shops and a municipal police station were damaged, while some protesters briefly forced their way into the lobby of City Hall. In Paris, police used tear gas and water cannons to push back people wearing hoods and masks and throwing fireworks and other objects at officers in the Place de la République, northeast of the Paris city center. Large numbers of riot police were deployed in the square and surrounding streets. The majority of peaceful protesters joined the march that started moving toward northwestern Paris. Protesters across France responded to calls on social media to revive the “yellow vest” movement, which emerged in 2018 against social injustice. Student groups protesting since mid-September through school blockades have urged supporters to join them. The CGT, one of France’s major labor unions, also backed the protests, calling for “higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services that meet people’s needs.” Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez’s office earlier said authorities had recorded 140 protest actions outside the Paris region by midday, involving over 30,000 people. Authorities reported at least 166 arrests across the country. Nuñez’s office pointed to violence carried out by people wearing masks in Paris, Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers. President Emmanuel Macron appealed Friday for calm. “There is a constitutional right to protest and to express oneself,” he said in Brussels. “But this right comes with the need to respect. Respect for people, respect for property, and therefore a commitment not to insult or destroy.” Police banned some other proposed gatherings in central Paris. Many metro stations were closed Saturday at police request, including those around the Champs-Elysées and near the presidential palace, parliament and government offices. In recent weeks, France has seen thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries and schools set on fire as the new school year descended into nationwide student protests that are influencing the country’s presidential election campaign and drawing international attention. Among protesters, particularly gruesome wounds suffered by some teenagers have been blamed on police riot-control weapons. Nuñez suspended the use of a type of police stun grenade against the young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand. On Tuesday, climate and social justice activist Greta Thunberg joined students at a high school in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis.

articles.title: Ilhan Omar’s lawyers demand the return of property seized in house raid
articles.summary: Omar’s legal team says the search violated safeguards designed to protect constitutional rights of members of Congress.
articles.body:
Lawyers for Democratic United States Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota have demanded the return of property seized in a federal raid of her Washington, DC home, accusing the US Department of Justice of conducting a politically motivated investigation and failing to follow judicial instructions during the search.

“The political motivations behind this pre-election investigation and search are clear as day,” Omar’s lawyers wrote in a letter sent to federal prosecutors on Friday and obtained by The Associated Press news agency. “This search was neither justified nor lawful.”

In the letter, Omar’s lawyers, Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, challenged an investigation into her immigration history, saying there was “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”.

The letter accuses federal agents of threatening the separation of powers and failing to comply with a magistrate judge’s instructions for the search of Omar’s northeast Washington home on Monday.

Federal agents searched Omar’s home on Monday as part of an investigation into alleged immigration fraud. Authorities seized her phone and passport, and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to The Washington Post. Her lawyers also asked authorities to preserve audio and video recordings from the search.

Omar’s lawyers claim that investigators did not provide a copy of the warrant to them in advance, nor did they contact the House of Representatives’ Office of General Counsel, which disregarded the magistrate judge’s orders. The notice would have allowed Omar to seek legal counsel and potentially leverage legislation that could have challenged the warrant.

Her lawyers said the procedures outlined by the judge are intended to protect Omar’s constitutional rights as a sitting member of Congress, and safeguard against the seizure of materials related to her legislative work.

Her lawyers also argued that the investigation was politically motivated due to its proximity to the November midterm elections.

“Historically, the Department has refrained from this type of investigative activity so close to an election, so as to avoid even the appearance of politically motivated law enforcement actions,” they wrote.

The Justice Department rejected the accusations, describing the letter as “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies”.

“Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do,” Justice Department spokesperson Emily Covington said.

Omar became a naturalised US citizen in 2000 after fleeing Somalia with her family as a child, according to her House biography. She has repeatedly rejected allegations by conservative critics about her immigration status, which was also probed in 2019 during Trump’s first administration.

Omar’s lawyers have requested records relating to the 2019 inquiry into her immigration history. The former investigation found insufficient evidence of wrongdoing to warrant a full investigation, according to The Washington Post.

The scope of the current investigation remains unclear.

The search took place days after Trump attacked Omar at a rally in Tennessee, describing her home country as a place of “crime and squalor” and suggesting that Vice President JD Vance and others were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump denied any involvement, telling reporters the matter was “really up to the DOJ”.

articles.title: 71-year-old man dies after alligator attack while fishing in Florida, police say
articles.summary: A 71-year-old man died after an alligator attacked him while he was fishing, authorities said on Friday.
articles.body: A 71-year-old man died after an alligator attacked him while he was fishing, authorities said on Friday. Steven Hamilton was fishing at Dr. Bradford Memorial Park in Winter Garden, Florida — a city about 15 miles west of Orlando — when he was bitten by an alligator, according to a statement from the Florida Fish & Wildlife Conservation Commission. Responding emergency personnel relayed reports that witnesses had seen someone possibly grabbed by an alligator and pulled into the water, according to a recording radio traffic. He was pronounced dead at the scene, the FWC said. The Winter Garden Police Department confirmed the incident in a statement, adding that FWC authorities trapped and killed the roughly 12-foot-long alligator. The FWC said that “serious injuries caused by alligators are rare in Florida.” In June, a 31-year-old woman died after an alligator bit off one of her arms and mauled the other at nearby Little Big Econ State Forest. “Always be aware of your surroundings. Always be safe,” Winter Garden police Capt. Michael Mason told reporters, according to NBC affiliate WESH 2 News. “Local wildlife, respect it, keep your distance. It looks like it’s docile, it looks like your Florida emblem, but it can be dangerous.” Mason encouraged witnesses of the incident to reach out to authorities.
